title: Fontaines D.C. New Album Review: Irish Band's Fifth LP Turns Darker and Bolder | Entertainment
text:
Fontaines D.C. release their fifth album, a darker, experimental record that follows Grammy nomination and sets up a 2025 stadium tour and Slane Castle headline slot.
Irish five-piece Fontaines D.C. have released their fifth album, arriving just seven years after they first emerged and barely a year after their 2020 debut, according to a new review. The band, once doubted as a commercially viable rock act in the 21st century, have now sold out a European arena tour that kicks off in Lisbon on Oct. 21, and will headline stadiums across the U.K. next year. In Ireland, they will play the 80,000-capacity Slane Castle, becoming the first domestic artist to headline the space since U2 in 2001.
Fontaines D.C. Album Follows Grammy-Nominated Success
The new record lands in an ongoing purple patch for the group. Their debut album came in 2020, a moodier offering than their loquacious first release, and in 2022 they returned with a third LP. They broke cover internationally with 2024's Grammy-nominated album, which channeled influences from grunge, nu-metal, and hip-hop. Sizzling tracks like Starburster and Bug travelled far and wide on platforms like TikTok, bringing them their biggest audiences yet. That LP landed at No. 97 on the U.S. charts.
The band's singer and primary lyricist, Grian Chatten, said he does not think every album needs balance. He noted that trying to always include light and shade on a track feels a bit cookie cutter. The new album's soundscape is suitably oblique, with nods to Depeche Mode, New Order, The Cure and Massive Attack. Its subject matter is bleaker still: dissociation, dissonance and despair. The LP takes on an even more tragic feel following a recent loss, according to the review.
Fontaines D.C. Sold-Out Tour and Stadium Ambitions
That overwhelming sense of dread has not put off fans. The group sold out their European arena tour, due to kick off in Lisbon on Oct. 21, in a matter of minutes. Next year, they will headline a number of stadiums across the U.K., and in Ireland they will take on the 80,000-capacity Slane Castle, becoming the first domestic artist to headline the space since U2 in 2001. The biggest names are now calling.
The album treads a fine line between introspection and darkness, with stadium-headlining ambition, and does so superbly, the review states. By the time of the record's closing moment, it is easy to feel overwhelmed by the sonic intensity and the sharpness and bleakness of the subject matter. Intimate comes as a fitting finale: not a neat summation, but more of a shellshocked whimper and acceptance that the world around us is unlikely to improve, so beauty must be found in pockets of everyday life.
Chatten sighs about what is inside helping to navigate a broken heart, before admitting that the ruins of the human dream make for a colourful ending and look so pretty in the final scene. The hulking lead single became the band's highest-charting single to date in the U.K., reaching No. 19 upon its arrival, prior to Fontaines' Reading and Leeds Festival headline slot in August. It showcases their grasp of dynamics and the need to build and release tension. As the atmosphere turns murkier and more discomfiting, synths splutter in and out of life; you could imagine it soundtracking a final girl's last-ditch escape in a horror film.
Fontaines D.C. Explores New Sonic Directions
As ever, Chatten's vocal is soft and lilting, though here he is not afraid to push it through odd, squelching, eerie effects. On Tongue, the second single issued from this LP, the band is lightyears away from their scrappy post-punk sound. Each song from their earlier album was anchored by an instinctive and catchy guitar riff from the off, but on Tongue you barely notice one kick in until the final 20 seconds. Instead there is a grooving bass line, skittish drum fills and a twinkling piano topline that shoots for the same sinister feel of Massive Attack's work. It is a sound that suits them, even if it feels less memorable than the rest of the material on this LP.
Self-realisation burns ferociously on the uncompromising One Man, which finds Chatten holding his notes like drones, flying outwards and enhancing the song's strange, spellbinding mood. It is topped off with disjointed acoustic guitar and spatters of ghostly electronics and drums, as Chatten sings of finding oneself, abandoning responsibilities, moving towards escapism and bathing in the feeling. He offers lines about forgetting worries and not being sorry if he failed someone.
The Rosalía team-up Where Is Gone? – the band's first-ever collaboration – ripples with dread, a combination of sonic dissonance and lyrics that contrast affection and intimacy with past hurt. It takes on the qualities of a future Bond theme as it rolls along: cinematic, muscular and faintly menacing, with quiet, simmering ferocity and sudden shifts between tension and calm, while Chatten and Rosalía trade vocals back and forth. At its centre is a purposefully ambiguous refrain asking where is gone and why the singer does not know, which adds a note of vulnerability. The lads have a knack for opening tracks, the review notes.
